analysis.one_liner: Reinstates the ban on exporting US-produced crude oil and natural gas, and lets the President restrict coal exports.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a committee referral: it was introduced with five Democratic senators behind it and died in the Senate Banking Committee when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the 2015 law that allowed US crude oil exports and direct the President to issue a rule banning exports of domestically produced crude oil and natural gas, with exemptions for cases the President finds consistent with the national interest. It would also give the President authority to restrict exports of coal, petroleum products, and petrochemical feedstocks, and to restrict shipments of materials and equipment needed for domestic energy production. Supporters framed it as keeping American energy at home for American consumers and cutting fossil fuel pollution; the bill received no committee action or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, US households could benefit if fuel produced in America stays in the American market instead of being shipped abroad, and communities exposed to fracking, pipelines, and export terminals would see less drilling and construction pressure. It would also serve climate goals by constraining the growth of US oil and gas output that exports enable.
analysis.who_benefits_short: US consumers and communities near fossil fuel infrastructure

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the President to issue a rule prohibiting the export of crude oil and natural gas produced in the United States, undoing the 2015 repeal of the decades-old export ban.

It gives the President power to restrict exports of coal, petroleum products, natural gas, and petrochemical feedstocks, and to restrict exports of materials and equipment needed for domestic energy production and construction of US energy facilities.

The bill includes safeguards for cross-border energy trade with Canada and Mexico and for transshipment arrangements, and allows the President to exempt exports he determines are in the national interest.
Enforcement would run through export-control procedures and penalties administered by the Commerce Secretary.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers and export terminal operators would lose access to foreign markets for US crude and LNG, which funds much of their US drilling activity. Coal producers could also face export restrictions. Consumers abroad would pay more for US fuel, and there is a real risk that cutting US producers off from world markets would shrink US production and raise domestic prices rather than lower them.

drawbacks.text: Economists widely credit the 2015 repeal of the crude export ban with expanding US oil production and lowering domestic gasoline prices; barring exports could shrink output and raise costs at the pump for the very consumers the bill aims to help.
The President's exemption authority is broad and discretionary, so the practical reach of the ban would depend entirely on who holds the office.
A unilateral US export ban could strain relations with allies that depend on US LNG, including European countries that shifted to American gas after cutting off Russian supply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's promise that keeping fuel at home lowers prices is disputed: the 2015 experience of lifting the ban cut domestic gasoline prices, so reinstating it could plausibly do the opposite while still delivering genuine climate and air-quality gains by restraining production. It is a blunt instrument with a real chance of backfiring on consumers, and its fate was sealed anyway by its narrow base of support.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced it, sent it to the Banking Committee on day one, and no one on the committee ever took it up before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the BAN Fossil Fuel Exports Act on May 18, 2023, joined by Senators Merkley, Sanders, Warren, and Wyden.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
That was the bill's last action: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas exporters, LNG terminal operators, and coal producers keep full access to foreign markets. Consumers got no change either way; the bill never came close to becoming law.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 1707 to reinstate the ban on US crude oil and natural gas exports.

for.name: Sens. Merkley, Sanders, Warren, and Wyden
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it five total Senate supporters.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote for the remaining nineteen months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Democrats or allied independents, and no Republicans cosponsored; there was never a vote to reveal how the chambers would have divided.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and export terminals
industries.note: A ban on crude and LNG exports would cut off their largest growth market and the revenue that finances new US drilling. Their interest in keeping exports flowing runs against the bill's aim of keeping fuel and reduced production at home.

The bill does not immediately ban coal exports but gives the President authority to restrict them, creating regulatory risk. Export restrictions on coal would align with climate and public-health goals.

If the ban held more domestic crude and gas in the US market, refiners and power providers could get cheaper feedstock, though reduced upstream production could offset that. Their potential gain would come alongside cheaper energy for households.
